title: Generative Drive Coach
description: UX case study: leading end-to-end design of Generative Drive Coach, a voice-first AI driving coach built at Woven by Toyota, from research through HMI and validation.

blocks.text: Owned end-to-end UX for Generative Drive Coach, spanning research, HMI and voice interaction design, prototyping, and validation.
Scaled a single teen-driving concept into a reusable coaching pattern system.
Patterns now cover parking, intersections, stop signs, turns, lane changes, and speed management, all built on the same voice-first coaching logic.
Grounded every design decision in Woven’s engineering stack:

items: CARLA: a proprietary driving simulator used to test coaching logic before real-world validation.
Vehicle SDK: real steering, speed, and sensor signals piped into working prototypes.
CAN signals: live vehicle bus data that grounded HMI behavior in actual driving state.

blocks.text: Rapidly translated feedback into working prototypes across Figma, simulator, and physical hardware:

items: Voice-enabled Figma flows: fast, low-fidelity concept testing.
CARLA simulator scenarios: realistic, repeatable driving conditions.
Physical steering & pedal rig: paired with updated HUD concepts for hands-on validation.

blocks.text: Owned research and validation end to end:

items: Study plans designed and run independently, start to finish.
Voice-frequency studies to tune how often and how loudly the coach should speak.
Simulated driving studies in CARLA to validate coaching behavior before road testing.
Iterative refinement of coaching behavior based on participant feedback.

blocks.text: I designed a voice-first coaching layer that delivers real-time, context-aware guidance without adding cognitive load, timed to the exact moment it’s needed: a stop sign, an intersection, a lane change. Voice-frequency studies shaped the interaction model, balancing how often the coach speaks against how much a new driver can actually absorb behind the wheel.
From Teen Driving to a Coaching System

What began as a single concept for coaching teen drivers became a reusable pattern system I built across parking, intersections, stop signs, turns, lane changes, and speed management.
Each pattern shares the same voice-first coaching logic, so adding a new driving scenario means composing existing building blocks, not starting from scratch. It’s a system, not a one-off feature.
A small token system — colors, type, spacing, and radii — kept the coaching HMI visually consistent from early dashboard mockups through CARLA test builds and the physical rig.
Each live component above is a real widget from the Flutter build. Toggle between SwiftUI, Flutter, and Tailwind to see the same pattern implemented natively across platforms.
A restrained palette tuned for daylight glare, night driving, and quick at-a-glance recognition.
Reserved for takeover alerts and destructive actions — used sparingly so it keeps its urgency.
A screen-legible type scale, sized and weighted for a quick glance at speed.
This is the standard body text used across paragraphs, general content blocks, and descriptive labels.
Consistent spatial rhythm across dashboard, HUD, and mobile companion surfaces.
Rounded surfaces calibrated to feel tactile on a touchscreen, not decorative.

To make coaching feel native to the car, I partnered with the software-integration and ML teams to ground the HMI in real vehicle state: pulling live signals from the Vehicle SDK and CAN bus into updated HUD concepts, so guidance stays synced to actual speed, position, and steering input, not a simulated approximation.

Working with the ML and research teams, I connected coaching designs to CARLA, Woven’s proprietary simulation platform, to run realistic driving scenarios and pressure-test coaching behavior before it ever touched a real vehicle.
From Figma to the Driver’s Seat

Feedback moved fast, so I kept prototypes moving just as fast: voice-enabled Figma flows for early concept testing, full simulator scenarios, and a physical rig with a real steering wheel and pedal controls.

Testing on physical controls surfaced timing and tone issues a screen-only prototype never would catch. Coaching that feels right in Figma can feel intrusive the moment your hands are actually on the wheel.
